appraisal_events.evidence: « Idiote, menteuse! s'écria-t-il »; « maquerelle, entremetteuse! »; the salon that had seemed to breathe « un goût vrai pour l'art » now « lui exhibait ses ridicules, sa sottise, son ignominie ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Fearing Odette will meet another man there freely, Swann violently reverses his earlier admiration and hurls insults at Mme Verdurin and her salon; the narrator marks his tone as theatrical ('factice') and his claimed noble mission to save Odette as an invention of the moment, framing the tirade as jealous self-dramatization rather than plain fact.

appraisal_events.evidence: « après lui avoir insinué adroitement quelques mots louangeurs pour Forcheville, comme elle avait fait si souvent pour lui »; « Vous allez faire une petite place à côté de vous à M. de Forcheville. »
appraisal_events.explanation: In Swann's anticipation of the next evening, Mme Verdurin will extend to Forcheville the same flattering notice and physical proximity to Odette she once reserved for Swann, comparatively elevating Forcheville into the favored place Swann fears losing. This is Swann's projected fantasy of a future scene, not a depicted event.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's tirade brands her stupid, lying, and a procuress, savagely lowering her local standing in his eyes.
The narrator undercuts Swann's grandiose self-justification (a supposed long-standing 'mission' to elevate Odette) as invented on the spot, exposing his righteous rhetoric as inflated and unreliable.
Consumed by jealousy, Swann dreads becoming the target of mockery and imagines being displaced from the confiding intimacy with Odette he formerly enjoyed.
In Swann's anticipation, Forcheville is drawn into favored proximity to Odette and flattering notice from Mme Verdurin, comparatively displacing Swann's former position.

ambiguities: The Chatou dinner, Mme Verdurin's favor toward Forcheville, and Odette's imagined mockery of Swann are all Swann's anticipatory fantasy rather than depicted events; the apparent certainty of Forcheville's rise and Swann's exclusion reflects his jealous projection, not confirmed narrative fact.
